goal: Teach Year-2 physics students to interpret a derivative as a physical rate, estimate vertical velocity with a forward difference, compare supplied step sizes, validate against an analytic derivative, state a simple error with units, and distinguish Core work from Working exposure.

deck_context.source_summary: Week 06 uses familiar vertical motion y(t)=20t-4.905t^2 to make numerical differentiation physical. The Core route is physical rate -> two nearby values -> forward difference -> pseudocode -> MATLAB scaffold -> step-size comparison -> analytic validation -> simple error -> physical interpretation. Central difference and the error curve are Working exposure only.
deck_context.core_claim: A numerical derivative estimates a physical rate from nearby values. It is credible only when its units, physical sign, analytic/reference check, and simple error are stated.
deck_context.locked_values: Forward estimates respectively: 7.7375, 9.2090, 9.6995, 9.94475 m/s. Corresponding absolute errors: 2.4525,0.9810,0.4905,0.24525 m/s. Corresponding relative errors: 24.0677%,9.6271%,4.8135%,2.4068%.
deck_context.scope_boundary: Do not require error-order derivations, detailed round-off analysis, higher-order formulas, or blank-page MATLAB coding. Central difference is supplied Working exposure, not Core implementation.

slides.title: From nearby values to an instantaneous rate
slides.intent: Open with a familiar projectile and a single driving question before formula vocabulary.
key_points: If a position model is known, how can two nearby values estimate the velocity at one instant?
slides.local_context: Use the exact vertical-position model y(t)=20t-4.905t^2. The curve must be an unmistakable concave-down y-versus-t parabola with exact visual anchors: begin at (0 s, 0 m); peak near (2.04 s, 20.39 m); cross y=0 again at t=4.08 s, visibly just to the right of the tick marked 4 and well before the tick marked 5. On a horizontal axis with ticks 0,1,2,3,4,5 s, place the dashed t0=1.0 s sample marker exactly vertical above the tick 1. A second marker t0+h must sit just to the right of it. It is a graph, not the ball's physical path: do not include a ball or any spatial-motion icon. Do not show numerical answer, code, central difference, or error theory.

layout.composition: sparse left title/question and a large accurate y-versus-t parabola on the right with two nearby time markers; optional small separate straight vertical-motion icon

visual_elements.main_visual: large labelled y-versus-t graph of the concave-down quadratic y(t)=20t-4.905t^2, with two close sample markers and one velocity-rate cue; never depict a ball or a spatial projectile trajectory

slides.source_image_rules: User-authorized exception: retain the approved ImageGen slide design, but replace the scientific graph region with a MATLAB-rendered plot of the locked model so exact coordinate anchors are preserved.
constraints: Do not introduce the forward-difference formula or a numerical result.

slides.title: A derivative is a physical rate
slides.intent: Connect derivative notation to familiar physical meanings and units.
key_points: position over time -> velocity in m/s
potential gradient dV/dx; electric field Ex = -dV/dx in V/m
temperature over time -> cooling rate in K/s
slides.local_context: Keep position -> velocity visually dominant; the other two are compact transfer examples. Distinguish the potential gradient dV/dx from the electric field Ex=-dV/dx. A derivative is not merely a symbol; it describes a change rate or gradient with units.

layout.composition: three horizontally aligned flat illustrated examples with arrows and unit badges

visual_elements.main_visual: three clear science mini-diagrams: rising ball, potential slope, cooling thermometer
visual_elements.supporting_elements: one navy derivative label above each mapping

constraints: Do not teach numerical formula yet; keep labels concise.

slides.title: Use two nearby values
slides.intent: Make forward difference a finite secant slope and distinguish it from a local tangent.
key_points: position change divided by time change
a secant estimates the tangent rate at t0
slides.local_context: Use a clean position-versus-time curve. Mark t0 and t0+h, two sampled points, a dusty-blue secant and a sage tangent reference. Numerator unit m, denominator unit s, result m/s. This colour mapping must also be used on Slide 12.

layout.composition: large flat graph-diagram with direct equation and three unit callouts

visual_elements.main_visual: position curve, two samples, forward secant and local tangent

slides.source_image_rules: Generate a conceptual diagram; preserve the exact formula.
constraints: No error-order theory; use textbook LaTeX-like math only for formula.

slides.title: Reuse a familiar vertical-motion model
slides.intent: Keep the physics familiar so the new cognitive load is the numerical method.
slides.local_context: Assume one-dimensional vertical motion under constant gravity with negligible air resistance. Show only a vertical height axis and upward motion at 1.0 s; do not depict horizontal travel, a projectile arc, or a two-dimensional trajectory. The model is equivalent to y(t)=20t-4.905t².

visual_elements.main_visual: ball moving vertically above a ground reference with height scale and direct variable labels

slides.title: Predict before computing
slides.intent: Establish a sign and magnitude expectation before numerical output appears.
key_points: At 1.0 s the projectile is still moving upward
velocity is less than the initial 20 m/s
slides.local_context: The expected analytic velocity later is 10.19 m/s, but do not show that number on this prediction slide. Focus on positive and below 20 m/s.

slides.title: Work one forward difference by hand
slides.intent: Show the unit-aware calculation for h=0.5 s.
slides.local_context: Reuse the user-approved sample image exactly; do not regenerate Slide 06.

slides.title: Pseudocode before MATLAB
slides.intent: Make the computational recipe explicit before code.
key_points: subtract, divide by h, compare with reference, repeat for supplied h values
slides.local_context: Present the exact sequence: choose t0/h -> evaluate y(t0) -> evaluate y(t0+h) -> subtract -> divide by h -> compare with reference -> repeat for next supplied h. No real programming syntax required.

layout.composition: left-to-right flat six-step flow with one loop-back arrow to supplied h list

visual_elements.main_visual: connected blue process arrows and small math/position icons

constraints: Keep wording short; no code block.

slides.title: Read the MATLAB scaffold line by line
slides.intent: Make students trace, not write from scratch, a concise supplied scaffold.
key_points: evaluate two positions then divide their difference by h_s
slides.local_context: Use this exact MATLAB excerpt: t0_s = 1.0; h_s = [0.5 0.2 0.1 0.05]; y_now_m = 20*t0_s - 4.905*t0_s^2; y_next_m = 20*(t0_s+h_s) - 4.905*(t0_s+h_s).^2; v_forward_mps = (y_next_m-y_now_m)./h_s;. Explain four callouts: TARGET, STEPS, TWO POSITIONS, DIVIDE BY STEP.

layout.composition: large readable dark-navy code panel with four flat coloured callouts arranged around it

visual_elements.main_visual: exact short MATLAB scaffold in monospaced visual style
visual_elements.supporting_elements: four direct arrows to exact code lines

slides.source_image_rules: Code text is strict teaching content.
constraints: Preserve element-wise .^ and ./ exactly; no long code or invented output.

slides.title: Why is the forward difference approximate?
slides.intent: Explain finite secant versus local tangent without truncation theory.
key_points: a forward difference uses a finite secant over h
the derivative is the local tangent rate
smaller h makes the secant more local, but h remains finite
slides.local_context: Use two side-by-side curved-function diagrams: coarse h with a visibly separated dusty-blue secant and sage tangent, and fine h with a dusty-blue secant closer to the same sage tangent. State that for a curved function such as this quadratic model, a forward difference is generally approximate; do not claim it is never exact, and do not say smaller h is universally better.

slides.title: Working exposure: a centred estimate
slides.intent: Show supplied central difference as breadth, clearly outside Core reproduction.
key_points: sample equally on both sides of t0
for this quadratic model it matches 10.19 m/s to floating-point precision
slides.local_context: Label Working exposure prominently but quietly. Show symmetric samples around t0. Use the exact formula [y(t0+h)-y(t0-h)]/(2h), with no stray punctuation. Include exact caveat: 'This special agreement is not guaranteed for every model.' Also mention a supplied error-versus-step-size view is interpretive only.

slides.title: Core transfer and exit ticket
slides.intent: Return explicitly to the Core route after the preceding Working-exposure slide, then close with transfer contexts and four compact recall prompts.
key_points: meaning, formula, step size, validation reference
slides.local_context: Place a clear 'CORE TRANSFER AND EXIT TICKET' badge at the top to distinguish this closing return to Core work from the preceding Working exposure. Show two flat transfer cards: Ex = -dV/dx with V/m; dT/dt with K/s. Ensure the temperature axis label is exactly T (K), never 7 (K). Finish with four prompts: What does the derivative mean? What is the forward-difference recipe? What changes when h is smaller? What is the validation reference? Do not reveal practical answers.
